result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.check_planarity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: >- Test planarity and return the evidence: an embedding or a Kuratowski subgraph. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.check_planarity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: >- Test planarity and return the evidence: an embedding or a Kuratowski subgraph. title: >- [Graph.check_planarity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Test planarity and return the evidence: an embedding or a Kuratowski subgraph. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Test planarity and return the evidence: an embedding or a Kuratowski subgraph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L20433-L20522){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.check_planarity(counterexample=False) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Check planarity](../assets/graphs/check-planarity.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: a wheel with hub 1 and rim 2 to 6, drawn so that going clockwise around the hub meets 2, 6, 5, 4, 3, which is the hub's entry in the embedding that check_planarity() returns with True. Right: the Petersen graph, which is not planar; check_planarity(True) returns False with a counterexample h, shown in the accent color: the graph without node 1 (dashed), a subdivided K3,3 whose six branch nodes are 3, 9, 10 and 4, 7, 8." width="100%"} Runs the same exact test as `is_planar()`, but also returns its certificate. For a planar graph that is a planar embedding (a rotation system): for every node, its neighbors in clockwise order around it in some drawing without edge crossings. Any straight-line or curved drawing that keeps these cyclic orders around every node can be made crossing-free; `layout_planar()` computes one. For a non-planar graph, with `counterexample=True`, it is a Kuratowski subgraph: a subdivision of `K_5` or `K_{3,3}`, which by Kuratowski's theorem is what every non-planar graph contains. This follows NetworkX's `check_planarity()`. Edge direction, self-loops and parallel edges are ignored, so each neighbor appears once in the embedding. NetworkX returns a `PlanarEmbedding` object; here the embedding is a plain dictionary of the same clockwise neighbor orders (`PlanarEmbedding.neighbors_cw_order()` in NetworkX). A graph usually has many planar embeddings, and the one returned here need not be the one NetworkX picks. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [counterexample]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, return a Kuratowski subgraph when the graph is not planar. Finding it reruns the planarity test once per edge, so it costs `O(e^2)` time; with `False` (default), `None` is returned instead. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tuple[bool, Optional[Union[dict[int, list[int]], Graph]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `(True, embedding)` if the graph is planar, where `embedding` maps each node ID to its neighbors' IDs in clockwise order (an empty list for an isolated node). `(False, None)` if it is not, or `(False, subgraph)` with `counterexample=True`: a new graph holding the Kuratowski subgraph's edges (for a pair of nodes joined by parallel edges, the one with the lowest ID) and their endpoints, with their IDs and attributes. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~is_planar`) : Just the yes-or-no answer. [](`~layout_planar`) : Positions that draw a planar graph without edge crossings. ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The embedding comes from the left-right planarity test, which assigns each back edge of a depth-first search to the left or right side of the tree and then orders the edges around each node by their nesting depth. For a connected graph, tracing the faces of the result gives the `e - n + 2` faces that Euler's formula requires of a planar drawing. The counterexample is found as NetworkX does: drop each edge in turn and put it back whenever the rest becomes planar. What remains is non-planar, but removing any one of its edges makes it planar, so it is a minimal non-planar subgraph, which can only be a subdivision of `K_5` or `K_{3,3}`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a planar embedding of a wheel, the neighbors of the hub (node `1`) come around it in the order of the rim, `2` to `6`: ::: {#31a58de0 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec wheel = ec.Graph().add_wheel_graph(6) planar, embedding = wheel.check_planarity() planar, embedding[1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (True, [2, 6, 5, 4, 3]) ``` ::: ::: The Petersen graph is not planar; the counterexample is a subdivision of `K_{3,3}` on nine of its ten nodes (six of them branch nodes of degree 3, three of them in the middle of a subdivided edge): ::: {#5990d0a5 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} petersen = ec.Graph().add_named_graph("petersen") planar, kuratowski = petersen.check_planarity(counterexample=True) planar, kuratowski.count_nodes(), kuratowski.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (False, 9, 12) ``` ::: :::
